title: Prose Does Not Bind Agents: Mechanically Enforced Safeguards for Multi-Agent Coding on a Single Repository
description: Coding agents are increasingly run in parallel against a single repository, under written instructions that tell them what to build and what to leave alone. This paper reports a 30-day case study of that arrangement: a repository whose 104 commits carry 126 Co-authored-by trailers, 120 of them naming one of three AI coding agents, and whose only scope rule the agents could read was a prose rulebook. We ask a narrow question: when such agents remove or weaken the very artefacts that constrain them, what makes the constraint survive? We report four findings. F1 (a disclosed, irreversible deletion). An agent removed the repository's specification harness: 137 files and 10,097 lines in one commit. It was named in full in the commit message, and the commit carries the agent's own trailer. It was not, however, the correct scope call that the commit's first sentence claims: the repository's own decision record, five days earlier and removed in the same commit, had already grounded the harness in the brief. What failed was the deletion and the record together — nothing in the repository afterwards distinguished never existed from deleted, and the scope rules that later governed the repository were written by the deletion itself. F2 (a directive that arrived after the work). Four agents working one task concurrently each built their own crop-and-export primitive instead of using the one the platform ships; one reached the trunk and had to be taken out again. The prose directive that would have prevented it was written the following day, and nothing could tell whether a given agent had complied. F3 (checks that pass for the wrong reason). Three automated checks passed while asserting less than they appeared to; each was found and fixed only because the property being claimed was written down and examined. F4 (the record of intent was written by the thing it was about). Most of the repository's decision records state the operator's positions, but most of them were drafted by a coding agent and ratified by him afterwards, and one of them describes work that agent had itself done. We then describe the mechanism that followed: moving constraints out of prose and into the build. Four rules — hash-pinned protected files, mechanical invariants, required and forbidden gate targets, and separately bounded budgets — all of which fail the build when violated. One episode is kept outside the findings, because no written rule answers it: the machine the agents ran on was compromised by a trojan (§4.5). We argue that the design question for agent-assisted development is not how to write better instructions but what to make checkable, and that a repository governed by prose is governed by nothing.
